questions.label: Using OOP inside project
questions.prompt: Explain how “Using OOP inside project” works in WiSe’s General section. Trace the trigger, the code or algorithm, and the resulting change in the game. Give one example and one edge case.
questions.summary: “OOP keeps each system responsible for its own behavior. The three characters share CharacterBase, ScriptableObjects hold editable starting data, and a HUD event channel tells listeners when live state changes.”

notes.heading: The four OOP pillars in your code
notes.text:
| Concept | Plain explanation | Your example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Encapsulation | Keep state behind methods that apply its rules. | CharacterBase keeps current HP/SP private. Heal, SpendSP, and Equip update them and notify the HUD. Some public fields still expose configuration directly, so encapsulation is selective. |
| Inheritance | A specific type reuses the common behavior of a parent. | WiSe, RandaL, and Druid inherit CharacterBase. NPC variants inherit NPCBase. |
| Abstraction | Expose a useful interface without requiring callers to know every implementation detail. | Item and NPCBase are abstract base classes. A shop can work with an Item reference. |
| Polymorphism | The same operation can behave differently for different types. | Equipment.Cost and Consumable.Cost override Item.Cost; NPC subclasses override approach/dialogue behavior. Consumable.Use(CharacterBase) is an overload, not an override of Use(). |

questions.label: Using Scriptable Object
questions.prompt: Why does WiSe use CharacterData ScriptableObjects?
questions.summary: “OOP keeps each system responsible for its own behavior. The three characters share CharacterBase, ScriptableObjects hold editable starting data, and a HUD event channel tells listeners when live state changes.”

notes.heading: How ScriptableObjects work here
notes.text: CharacterData stores starting stats. Item, Equipment, BattleSkill, DungeonSettings, and audio settings store editable asset data. A .cs file defines the shape; a .asset file contains a configured instance. Runtime HP, EXP, and ultimate unlocks belong to the character instance, so unlocking a skill does not rewrite the shared starting asset.

questions.label: Using Event Channel
questions.prompt: What is the purpose of CharacterHudEventChannel?
questions.summary: “OOP keeps each system responsible for its own behavior. The three characters share CharacterBase, ScriptableObjects hold editable starting data, and a HUD event channel tells listeners when live state changes.”

notes.heading: How the HUD event channel works
notes.text:
1. A stat method changes the character.
2. NotifyStatsChanged raises CharacterStatsChanged on the assigned channel.
3. HUD scripts subscribed to that asset update their display.
4. Selection uses the separate CharacterSelected event.

notes.heading: How the HUD event channel works
notes.text: The publisher does not need to know which HUD is listening. Both sides must use the same event-channel asset. Subscribe in OnEnable and unsubscribe in OnDisable to avoid stale listeners. IntEventChannel is another available channel type; its existence alone does not prove a particular scene uses it.

questions.label: Responsive UI
questions.prompt: How would you demonstrate “Responsive UI” in WiSe’s General section? Describe the setup, what the player should see or hear, and what would count as a failure.
questions.summary: “Audio uses shared mixer routing and movement distance determines steps. Visual cues reflect actual gameplay state, while scene assets provide the specific particles, outlines, and post processing.”

notes.heading: Responsive UI and post processing
notes.text: Scenes contain Unity UI and global Volume objects; BattleScene has its own post-processing object. Anchors, CanvasScaler configuration, text sizing, and actual resolution determine layout. Merely using RectTransform does not establish that every screen is responsive. Inspect each major overlay at different supported aspect ratios.

notes.heading: Responsive UI and post processing
notes.text: Visual feedback is separate from gameplay permission: a shield icon must agree with BattleUnit.shields, a door highlight must agree with lock/key state, and a blended shore must agree with WFC terrain. Asset/scene assignments determine whether the authored clips/materials actually appear in a player build.

notes.heading: Git and GitHub
notes.text: The inspected repository contains commits about enemy patrols/attacks, boss projectile speed, travel transitions, arrival feedback, Berdly animation, and dungeon generation limits. This shows local history. This documentation review did not inspect GitHub push timing, so “push periodically” needs remote evidence if assessed.

notes.heading: Git and GitHub
notes.text: Git records version history locally: working files → staged changes → commit. A branch is a movable label for a line of commits. GitHub hosts repositories for sharing, remote backup, and review. A commit can exist locally without being pushed to GitHub.

questions.label: Show title
questions.prompt: How would you demonstrate “Show title” in WiSe’s UI section? Describe the setup, what the player should see or hear, and what would count as a failure.
questions.summary: “Play chooses a save slot. Empty means a fresh playthrough, occupied means restore. Continue uses last-played time, and the fade hides initialization.”

notes.heading: What the player sees
notes.text: TitleScene contains the title, Play/save-slot flow, Continue Last Played, Settings, and Exit. Title audio plays looping music and one-shot button sounds.

notes.heading: How it works
notes.text:
1. Play exposes the saved slot cards through the title UI wiring.
2. SaveSlotUI.SelectSlot checks whether the chosen file exists.
3. An empty slot calls GameSave.TryStartNewGame; a valid occupied slot calls TryLoadSlot.
4. A fade covers scene loading and restoration.
5. Continue chooses the valid slot with the latest last-played timestamp.
6. Settings shows its overlay. Exit delegates to the exit component.

questions.demo: Start TitleScene. Open Play, inspect all three cards, return, open Settings, and use Continue if a valid save exists. Check the actual title character display and Play animation separately. Deleting a card is optional and destroys that slot's progress.

questions.label: Save using binary
questions.prompt: Explain how “Save using binary” works in WiSe’s Save File section. Trace the trigger, the code or algorithm, and the resulting change in the game. Give one example and one edge case.
questions.summary: “Capture makes a data snapshot, the binary writer stores an explicit versioned schema with a corruption checksum, and loading restores the seed before generating the world.”

notes.heading: Saving, step by step
notes.text:
1. GameSave.Capture converts live scene state into plain SaveData.
2. Items/equipment are recorded by names resolved through the item catalog.
3. BinarySaveFile.Write validates the data and writes primitives/arrays in a fixed order.
4. A header stores WISE, schema version 3, payload length, and SHA-256 checksum.
5. The complete temporary file replaces the prior file. Save & Quit returns to the title only after a successful write.

notes.heading: Loading, step by step
notes.text: Version 2 binary saves are readable. A legacy version 1 JSON file has a one-time import path. A checksum detects corruption; it is not encryption or proof a file has not been deliberately edited.

notes.heading: What this ability does
notes.text: WiSe is the exploration character for destructive interactions. Trees/cactus produce resource pickups; dungeon breakables use a timed swing/impact and may drop coins.

notes.heading: How tree cutting works
notes.text: WiSe.Update reads F directly through Input System's Keyboard.current and searches for a suitable nearby TreeCuttable. It coordinates the character's breaking animation with the cut. TreeCuttable.Cut checks a cut guard, creates its configured loot, disables colliders, requests navigation rebuilding, and destroys the object.

questions.label: RandaL summoning book

notes.heading: What the player sees
notes.text: With RandaL selected, F toggles placement mode. The ghost book turns green on a valid location and red on an invalid location. Left-click commits a valid placement; F cancels.

notes.heading: Placement checks, in order
notes.text:
1. A usable camera and mouse exist and the cursor is inside the camera view.
2. A solid hit exists; a filled hit buffer is rejected conservatively.
3. The hit is within the maximum distance from RandaL.
4. Its layer and slope are allowed. In the active overworld it must be a TerrainCollider.
5. The preview's visible bounds produce an overlap box.
6. Other solid objects must not overlap that box; a filled overlap buffer is rejected.

questions.label: Show every item in the shop

questions.summary: “The shop calculates quantity × price and spends gold before adding copies. Merchants buy only their assigned resource. Diamond is filtered through consumable cost data.”

notes.heading: Buying, step by step
notes.text:
1. InteractableNPC opens the ShopInventory assigned to it.
2. ShopUI creates a button for each eligible entry and selects an item.
3. Quantity is clamped between 1 and the configured maximum (class default 99).
4. Total cost is price × quantity, calculated with a long integer before checking the supported gold range.
5. SpendGold must succeed before items are added.
6. One inventory copy is added per purchased unit, and the gold UI refreshes.

notes.heading: What the player sees
notes.text: A shop offers a grid, selected name/description, quantity controls, total cost, gold, and Buy. A resource merchant buys one configured resource type.

questions.label: Algorithm Implementation
questions.prompt: In WiSe’s WFC generation, what happens after a terrain option is chosen for a cell?
questions.summary: “Each cell has allowed terrain options. We collapse the lowest weighted entropy cell, propagate neighbor rules, and instantiate the selected Terrain prefab. The seed reproduces choices; the inset pool pattern preserves the shore.”

notes.heading: What WFC does
notes.text: Wave Function Collapse chooses terrain while respecting allowed neighboring types. A cell begins with a set of possible tiles, called its domain. Collapsing chooses one option; propagation removes incompatible options from nearby cells.

notes.heading: The algorithm in your code
notes.text:
1. Choose the seeded pool pattern for a chunk independently of collapse retries.
2. Begin other cells with LandMask.
3. Reserve the 5×5 water interior, a sand ring, and then a grass/rock ring.
4. Propagate all initial domains through the eight neighbors, including diagonals.
5. FindLowest chooses the unresolved cell with lowest weighted Shannon entropy.
6. PickTerrain makes a weighted seeded choice among allowed options.
7. Propagate again until every cell is resolved.
8. On contradiction, retry deterministically, up to 16 attempts; exhaustion throws instead of silently replacing water-adjacent cells with grass.
9. Instantiate tiles[tile], the assigned prefab selected by WFC.

questions.label: Dungeon Generation
questions.prompt: Which pipeline creates the dungeon room graph in WiSe?
questions.summary: “A random walk supplies positions, Kruskal builds a connected tree, recursive naming selects chains, and progression rules assign keys/locks. A separate WFC decorates each room's floor.”

notes.heading: Room graph generation
notes.text:
1. A seeded random walk collects adjacent grid positions.
2. All orthogonally adjacent positions become possible edges with random weights.
3. Kruskal's algorithm sorts edges and uses disjoint sets to reject cycles, producing a minimum spanning tree.
4. The naming algorithm selects the main chain and recursively selects branches.
5. Each room gets a chain index, one-based position, chain degree, random size, and initial kind.
6. The first main-chain room becomes Spawn, the second Guide/Berdly, and the last Boss.
7. Progression keys and door locks are assigned, then the shared chemistry algorithm produces the dungeon name.

notes.heading: Two different generation jobs
notes.text: DungeonLayout makes the room/door graph and progression data. DungeonGenerator builds rooms and contents from that data. DungeonFloorWFC chooses each room's floor tiles. The floor WFC does not decide the entire dungeon room graph.

notes.heading: What the player opens
notes.text: Esc opens the gameplay menu. MenuTabManager selects the default tab and switches between configured panels. Items, equipment, resources, stats, audio settings, and quit each have a separate UI owner.

notes.heading: Panel responsibilities
notes.text:
- InventoryUI selects consumables and their character targets, validates use, and refreshes quantities/HP/SP.
- EquipmentUI selects gear/slots and shows stat differences.
- ResourceMenuPanelUI reads resource counts from Inventory; it does not generate world resources.
- StatsMenuPanelUI reads CharacterBase's current/base-plus-equipment stats.
- GameAudioMenuUI changes shared audio settings.
- QuitMenuUI offers Keep Playing or Save & Quit and displays save failures.
- MenuStatBar applies current values and preview presentation to the configured UI bars.

notes.heading: The turn model
notes.text: Press T to end the party turn. Each living enemy resets movement, chooses the closest living target, moves within its range, and attacks. Party turns reset AP/movement and advance character cooldowns. Cooldowns are stored on CharacterBase and persist between battles.

notes.heading: The turn model
notes.text: Player, Enemy, Acting, Victory, and GameOver are separate phases. You can switch living characters during the party turn. Each has a movement origin/radius and two AP. Skill/ultimate slots spend one AP; basic attack spends no AP but locks movement. SP, cooldown, phase, living state, and unlock gates also control usability.

notes.heading: What an FSM is
notes.text: A finite state machine chooses one named state and performs that state's behavior. Your encounter enemy has Idle, Patrol, Chase, Attack, and OutOfSight. Transitions reset relevant timers and pending attack impact.

notes.heading: What an FSM is
notes.text:
| State | Behavior and exit |
| --- | --- |
| Idle | Waits stationary; after three seconds, tries a patrol destination. |
| Patrol | Moves toward a seeded random reachable point near home; returns to Idle on arrival/timeout. |
| Chase | Repaths toward the detected player. |
| Attack | Stops, faces the player, winds up, and checks/launches an impact. |
| OutOfSight | Stops and visibly searches left/right; returns to Idle after about 1.5 seconds. |

notes.heading: One turn

notes.text: PinkRhythmController schedules music/countdown and uses the audio DSP clock to advance play. It supplies pressed/held key masks to the rules. UI note positions are drawn from note time versus current time, and a visual pool reuses note objects. timingOffset is the configurable alignment adjustment.

notes.heading: What the player does
notes.text: Accept Pink's challenge and use W/A/S/D as notes reach the target. Tap notes need a press; hold notes need a press followed by sustained input. The UI shows score, judgement, stamina, moving notes, and the Mario/Pink stage model.

notes.heading: Beatmap format
notes.text: PinkBeatmap.Parse requires a start= audio offset and a notes= count. 1 t=1000 is a W tap at one second. 2 tstart=2000 tend=3500 is an A hold from two to 3.5 seconds. notes.text: The maximum selected chain is 11. LongestChainLength uses tree-distance searches to detect the diameter length, but the actual tie-breaking chain selection comes from BestPath. Do not confuse the longest-length helper with the full numbering algorithm.

notes.heading: Naming, step by step
notes.text:
1. BestPath considers possible endpoints within the selected component.
2. Prefer the longest chain, then branch/locant tie-breaks.
3. For the top-level chain consider orientation so branch locants favor the earlier/lower arrangement.
4. For each off-chain connected component, recursively call NamePart from its attachment root.
5. Group identical branch names, collect their one-based positions, and apply multiplier prefixes.
6. Sort branch-name groups and append the parent alkane from the naming table.
7. A nested branch name is wrapped in parentheses using the project's recursive notation.

questions.label: WFC oral Question 1
questions.prompt: Walk through one WFC collapse: initial domains, entropy, weighted selection, propagation, contradiction handling, and prefab instantiation.
questions.summary: Begin with allowed domains, choose the lowest weighted-entropy unresolved cell, make a seeded weighted pick, propagate constraints, retry deterministic contradictions, and instantiate the selected assigned Terrain prefab.
questions.answer: Begin with allowed domains, choose the lowest weighted-entropy unresolved cell, make a seeded weighted pick, propagate constraints, retry deterministic contradictions, and instantiate the selected assigned Terrain prefab.

notes.heading: What WFC does
notes.text: Wave Function Collapse chooses terrain while respecting allowed neighboring types. A cell begins with a set of possible tiles, called its domain. Collapsing chooses one option; propagation removes incompatible options from nearby cells.

notes.heading: The algorithm in your code
notes.text:
1. Choose the seeded pool pattern for a chunk independently of collapse retries.
2. Begin other cells with LandMask.
3. Reserve the 5×5 water interior, a sand ring, and then a grass/rock ring.
4. Propagate all initial domains through the eight neighbors, including diagonals.
5. FindLowest chooses the unresolved cell with lowest weighted Shannon entropy.
6. PickTerrain makes a weighted seeded choice among allowed options.
7. Propagate again until every cell is resolved.
8. On contradiction, retry deterministically, up to 16 attempts; exhaustion throws instead of silently replacing water-adjacent cells with grass.
9. Instantiate tiles[tile], the assigned prefab selected by WFC.

questions.prompt: How do seeds and chunk coordinates give reproducible worlds without breaking shorelines at diagonal corners or chunk borders?

notes.heading: What WFC does
notes.text: Wave Function Collapse chooses terrain while respecting allowed neighboring types. A cell begins with a set of possible tiles, called its domain. Collapsing chooses one option; propagation removes incompatible options from nearby cells.

notes.heading: The algorithm in your code
notes.text:
1. Choose the seeded pool pattern for a chunk independently of collapse retries.
2. Begin other cells with LandMask.
3. Reserve the 5×5 water interior, a sand ring, and then a grass/rock ring.
4. Propagate all initial domains through the eight neighbors, including diagonals.
5. FindLowest chooses the unresolved cell with lowest weighted Shannon entropy.
6. PickTerrain makes a weighted seeded choice among allowed options.
7. Propagate again until every cell is resolved.
8. On contradiction, retry deterministically, up to 16 attempts; exhaustion throws instead of silently replacing water-adjacent cells with grass.
9. Instantiate tiles[tile], the assigned prefab selected by WFC.

| Mechanism | What work it reduces | Tradeoff to explain |

notes.heading: Room graph generation
notes.text:
1. A seeded random walk collects adjacent grid positions.
2. All orthogonally adjacent positions become possible edges with random weights.
3. Kruskal's algorithm sorts edges and uses disjoint sets to reject cycles, producing a minimum spanning tree.
4. The naming algorithm selects the main chain and recursively selects branches.
5. Each room gets a chain index, one-based position, chain degree, random size, and initial kind.
6. The first main-chain room becomes Spawn, the second Guide/Berdly, and the last Boss.
7. Progression keys and door locks are assigned, then the shared chemistry algorithm produces the dungeon name.

notes.heading: Room graph generation
notes.text: The configured default range in DungeonSettings is 14–24 rooms. A selected parent chain is limited to 11 rooms, even when the whole graph has more. Bounded retries reject unsuitable graphs and enforce enough branching for larger dungeons.
